introduction-why-do-we-need-locks.core: Distributed locks ensure only one process acts on a resource at a time across machines: one cron runner, one writer to a file, one processor per account. Locks serve efficiency (avoid duplicate work, where an occasional double is fine) or correctness (must never overlap, which needs consensus plus fencing). Knowing which you need decides the implementation.

first_principles.problem: A team uses a Redis lock to protect financial updates and occasionally double-applies them.
derivation: Prefer **idempotency or transactions** over locks where possible.

analogy.title: A single key to a shared tool shed
analogy.story: Mostly it stops two people using the saw at once; for dangerous machinery you also need a logbook check.
analogy.breaks: Keys can't be duplicated by time passing; locks can expire while the holder still thinks it has them.

example.title: Choosing an approach
flow: Daily report job → Redis SET NX PX (efficiency)
Account balance updates → DB transaction or etcd lock + fencing
Event processing → partition by key, no lock

check.q: Why distinguish efficiency locks from correctness locks?
check.a: Efficiency locks tolerate rare overlaps and can be simple; correctness locks must never overlap and need consensus plus fencing.

the-lease-mechanism.core: Distributed locks are leases: they expire automatically after a TTL so a crashed holder doesn't block others forever. The holder must finish or renew before expiry. The trade-off: short TTLs recover faster from crashes but risk expiring during long operations or pauses; long TTLs delay recovery.

first_principles.problem: A worker crashes holding a lock with no expiry, and the job is blocked until someone notices.
derivation: Release **explicitly** when done (only if still owner).

analogy.title: Renting a locker by the hour
analogy.story: If you don't come back, it's cleared automatically; if you need more time, you pay to extend.
analogy.breaks: Locker staff warn you; distributed leases expire silently.

branches.label: Trade-off
children: Short TTL: fast recovery, expiry risk

code.text:
-- release only if we still own the lock
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end

check.q: Why must lock release check ownership?
check.a: The lock may have expired and been acquired by someone else, whose lock you'd otherwise delete.

redlock-distributed-locking-with-redis.core: Redlock acquires a lock on a majority of N independent Redis masters (e.g. 3 of 5) within a time limit, using SET key random NX PX ttl on each, and considers the lock held for the remaining validity time. It improves availability over a single Redis but, as Martin Kleppmann argued, relies on timing assumptions (bounded pauses and drift) and provides no fencing tokens, so it's unsafe for correctness-critical locking.

first_principles.problem: A team adopts Redlock believing it guarantees mutual exclusion under all conditions.
truths: No monotonic token means no fencing.
derivation: Use Redlock for **efficiency locks** at most.
Prefer a **single Redis + simple lock** if failover risk is acceptable.

analogy.title: Getting permission from three of five managers by phone within a minute
analogy.story: Usually fine, but if a call is delayed or you fall asleep mid-task, two people may both think they're approved.
analogy.breaks: Managers keep records; Redis keys just expire.

example.title: Failure scenario
flow: Client 1 wakes and writes, with no token to reject it

check.q: What key safety feature does Redlock lack?
check.a: Monotonic fencing tokens to reject stale lock holders.

the-danger-of-clock-drift.core: Time-based locks assume clocks advance at similar rates and processes don't pause unexpectedly. In reality clocks drift, NTP can step time, VMs migrate and GC pauses last seconds. Any of these can make a lock holder believe its lease is valid after others see it expired, so overlapping holders are possible without fencing.

first_principles.problem: A Redis server's clock jumps forward after an NTP correction, expiring a lock early while its holder is mid-operation.
truths: Pauses aren't observable by the paused process.
TTLs depend on clocks on both sides.
derivation: Never rely on **time alone** for correctness.

analogy.title: Two people timing the same hourglass from different rooms
analogy.story: If one room's clock is off, they disagree on when time is up.
analogy.breaks: Hourglasses don't jump; system clocks can be stepped by NTP.

example.title: Overlap from a clock jump
flow: Lock TTL 10 s set at server time 100
Second client acquires while first still working

check.q: Why can a GC pause break a time-based lock?
check.a: The holder doesn't notice time passing, so it may act after the lock has expired and been granted to someone else.

consensus-based-locking-zookeeper-and-et.core: Consensus stores give correctness-grade locks: ZooKeeper's ephemeral sequential znodes (lowest sequence holds the lock, others watch their predecessor, the lock vanishes when the session dies) and etcd's leases with revision-ordered keys (concurrency.Mutex). Both provide monotonic numbers (zxid, revision) usable as fencing tokens.

first_principles.problem: A payment reconciliation job must never run twice concurrently, even during failures.
truths: Consensus gives a single consistent view.
derivation: **etcd**: lease + key with revision; lowest revision wins.
Avoid **herd effect** by watching predecessor only.

analogy.title: A numbered queue at a government office
analogy.story: Your ticket number is your place; if you leave, your ticket is void, and only the counter's current number is served.
analogy.breaks: Government queues are slow; consensus locks are acquired in milliseconds.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Exclusive execution with a fencing token.

code.text:
s, _ := concurrency.NewSession(cli, concurrency.WithTTL(10))
m := concurrency.NewMutex(s, "/locks/reconcile")
if err := m.Lock(ctx); err != nil { return err }
token := m.Header().Revision          // fencing token
runReconcile(ctx, token)
m.Unlock(ctx)

check.q: How does a ZooKeeper lock avoid the herd effect?
check.a: Each waiter watches only its immediate predecessor znode rather than the lock holder.
